claims.claim: The Situation-Behaviour-Impact (SBI) model was developed by the Center for Creative Leadership; its extension adds Intent; it suits positive and negative feedback.
claims.source: Mind Tools and several secondary sources found by search on 13 November 2026; ccl.org was not reachable from the build environment.

claims.claim: The steps for receiving feedback and asking narrow questions are common practice.
claims.source: General practice, not a quotation from one source.

concept_html:
Vague feedback changes nothing. "Your presentation was a bit messy" leaves the other person guessing what to fix, and "great job" does not tell them what to repeat. The Situation-Behaviour-Impact model from the Center for Creative Leadership (CCL) makes feedback specific.

The three parts.

  • Situation: when and where. "In Tuesday's steering group, when you presented the attrition model."
  • Behaviour: what the person did, described so a camera could have recorded it. "You spent ten minutes on feature engineering before showing the result." Leave out judgements such as "messy" or "rude". They describe your reaction, not the act.
  • Impact: the effect on you, the group or the outcome, as an "I" statement. "I saw the HR director check their phone, and we ran out of time for the decision."

Add intent and listen. CCL's extension adds a fourth step: ask what the person was trying to do. "What were you aiming for with the detail?" Their answer often changes your view, and it turns the feedback into a conversation.

Use it for praise too. "In the board pack, you put the recommendation in the subject line. The CFO approved it the same day." Specific praise shows what to repeat.

Receiving feedback. Listen to the end without defending yourself. Ask for a specific example. Thank the person. Then decide what you will act on, and tell them later what you changed.

Ask well. "Any feedback?" gets "all fine". Ask a narrow question instead: "What one thing should I change in how I present findings?"

notes.html: When and where, so the person knows exactly which moment you mean.
What a camera would have recorded. No judgement words.
Asking about intent turns feedback into a conversation.

example.takeaway_html: Give feedback as situation, behaviour and impact. Describe what a camera would see, state the effect as an "I" statement, and ask about intent. Use it for praise as well as for change.

- Situation, behaviour and impact give them something specific to fix.
- Asking about intent finds the cause, which might be a deadline, not carelessness.

title: Give and receive feedback with situation, behaviour and impact
why_html: A lead told an analyst that their reports "lacked polish". The analyst spent a month on fonts and colours. The lead had meant that the reports buried the answer. "In last week's report, the recommendation was on page four, and the director missed it" would have fixed it in one draft.
